> **What this case shows** — the [Granger case](../granger-cardioresp-bidmc/index.qmd) measured
> *directed* coupling by fitting a **linear** autoregression. **Transfer entropy** (Schreiber
> 2000) measures the same directed influence **without a model**: it is the reduction in
> uncertainty about one signal's future gained from another's past, beyond its own past, in bits —
> so it captures *nonlinear* directed coupling too. On real cardiorespiratory signals the
> model-free **respiration → pulse** transfer entropy (**0.036 bits**) exceeds **pulse →
> respiration** (**0.024**), net **+0.012** — the same directed asymmetry the linear Granger
> analysis found. And the estimate is exact: `transferEntropy` (histogram estimator) reproduces an
> independent from-scratch numpy transfer entropy **bit-for-bit** (max |diff| ~ 6e-17), and it
> recovers a constructed directed coupling (x drives y → TE **0.67** in the driving direction vs
> **0.06** reverse).

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — for model-free directed coupling: `transferEntropy(x, y, sr, estimator = "histogram")`
→ read the two directions and their difference (the net directed information flow).
**Way of thinking** — transfer entropy is the *model-free* complement of Granger causality:
Granger asks "does x's past improve a *linear* forecast of y?"; transfer entropy asks "does x's
past reduce the *uncertainty* of y at all?" — no linearity assumed. When the two agree, the
coupling is (at least partly) linear; where transfer entropy sees coupling Granger misses, it is
nonlinear.
**Ecosystem usage** — `PhysioCrossModal::transferEntropy()`; `estimator = "ksg"` for the
less-biased kNN estimator, `effective = TRUE` for surrogate-corrected significance.
:::

## Proposition

On real cardiorespiratory signals (BIDMC-01), the model-free respiration → pulse transfer entropy
(0.036 bits) exceeds pulse → respiration (0.024), net +0.012; `transferEntropy` reproduces an
independent numpy transfer entropy bit-for-bit (~6e-17); and it recovers a constructed x → y
coupling (TE 0.67 driving vs 0.06 reverse).

## Question & goal

**The question is direction, without assuming linearity: does respiration drive the pulse more
than the pulse drives respiration — measured model-free — and does the ecosystem compute transfer
entropy exactly?** Granger answers it under a linear model; transfer entropy answers it with no
model at all. The goal is a machine-precision validation, a ground-truth directed-recovery check,
and a read of the real directed information flow.

## Challenge & approach

Transfer entropy is only as trustworthy as its estimator, and estimators disagree. We pin the one
we validate: the histogram estimator, with equal-width binning. We compute it with
`transferEntropy`, re-compute it from scratch in numpy (matched embedding + binning + the Schreiber
formula, in a different language), and confirm the measure identifies the driver on a constructed
coupling where the answer is known.

```
RESP, PLETH (BIDMC, 25 Hz) → transferEntropy(histogram, bins = 8) → TE both directions, net +0.012
                    vs independent from-scratch numpy transfer entropy → bit-exact (~6e-17)
      constructed x→y coupling → transferEntropy                     → TE 0.67 driving vs 0.06 reverse
```

## Data

**BIDMC PPG and Respiration Dataset (PhysioNet)**: subject **bidmc01**, **respiration** (RESP) and
**PPG** (PLETH) decimated 125 → 25 Hz, 200 s — the same git-tracked pair the sibling
[Granger case](../granger-cardioresp-bidmc/index.qmd) uses. Details in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![Left: the model-free directed information flow in both directions — respiration → pulse (0.036 bits) exceeds pulse → respiration (0.024), a net +0.012 directed asymmetry; the op (bars) and the independent numpy transfer entropy (points) coincide. Right: the op-minus-numpy residual, at the ~1e-17 floating-point floor in both directions — a bit-exact match — with the constructed-coupling recovery (TE 0.67 driving vs 0.06 reverse) annotated.](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* the left panel is the finding (respiration leads the pulse in model-free
directed information); the right panel is the validation (op = numpy to the floating-point floor,
and the measure recovers a known driver).

| Quantity | Value |
|---|--:|
| transfer entropy **respiration → pulse** (bits) | **0.0358** |
| transfer entropy **pulse → respiration** (bits) | **0.0240** |
| **net (respiration → pulse) — directed asymmetry** | **+0.0118** |
| op vs independent numpy (max \|diff\|) | **6e-17** (bit-exact) |
| constructed coupling: TE **driving** direction | **0.668** |
| constructed coupling: TE **reverse** direction | **0.064** |

The op matches numpy to the floating-point floor in both directions, correctly identifies the
driver of a constructed coupling, and on the real pair measures a weak respiration → pulse directed
information flow — consistent with the Granger result. Values trace to
[`artifacts/te_summary.csv`](artifacts/te_summary.csv).

## Conclusion

The ecosystem's transfer entropy is the exact histogram transfer entropy — bit-for-bit against an
independent numpy implementation — it recovers a known directed coupling, and on real
cardiorespiratory signals it measures, *without a model*, the same respiration-leads-pulse
asymmetry the linear Granger analysis found. The transferable takeaway: **reach for transfer
entropy when you can't assume linearity; pin the estimator (this validates the histogram one — the
KSG estimator gives different absolute values); read the *net* of the two directions; and treat
small absolute values as biased point estimates, not significance tests — use `effective = TRUE`
for that.**

## Open questions

- This uses the histogram estimator (fast, positively biased); the **KSG/kNN** estimator
  (`estimator = "ksg"`, also implemented) is less biased for continuous data, and the
  **effective** transfer entropy (`effective = TRUE`, surrogate-corrected) tests significance
  against IAAFT surrogates. Computing the effective KSG transfer entropy across a cohort — and
  comparing its directed map to the linear Granger map — would show *where the coupling is
  genuinely nonlinear*. *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| Step | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| model-free directed coupling (both directions) | `transferEntropy()` | PhysioCrossModal |
| less-biased kNN estimator | `transferEntropy(estimator = "ksg")` | PhysioCrossModal |
| surrogate-corrected significance | `transferEntropy(effective = TRUE)` | PhysioCrossModal |
| linear directed coupling (the complement) | `grangerCausality()` | PhysioCrossModal |

**Choosing the parameters.**

- **estimator** — `"histogram"` (validated here; fast, equal-width binning, positively biased) vs
  `"ksg"` (Kraskov–Stögbauer–Grassberger kNN; less biased for continuous data, different absolute
  scale).
- **bins** — for the histogram estimator, the number of equal-width bins per embedding coordinate
  (here 8); more bins resolve finer structure but worsen the finite-sample bias.
- **k, l, delay** — the embedding: `k` past lags of the target, `l` past lags of the source, and
  the prediction `delay` (here 1, 1, 1 — a one-step Markov embedding).
- **effective** — `TRUE` subtracts the transfer entropy of IAAFT surrogates, turning the biased
  raw value into a significance-tested effective transfer entropy.

**The recipe, copy-runnable:**

```r
library(PhysioCrossModal)

te <- transferEntropy(resp, pleth, sr = 25, estimator = "histogram", bins = 8)
te$te_xy   # respiration -> pulse (bits)
te$te_yx   # pulse -> respiration
te$te_xy - te$te_yx   # net directed information flow: +0.012 (respiration leads)

# reproduces an independent from-scratch numpy transfer entropy bit-for-bit (~6e-17);
# recovers a constructed x->y coupling (TE 0.67 driving vs 0.06 reverse).
```

**Auditing the numbers.** Every value on this page traces to
[`artifacts/te_summary.csv`](artifacts/te_summary.csv), and [`audit.py`](audit.py) re-checks each
number, the numpy bit-exact match in both directions, the constructed-coupling directed recovery,
the internal net consistency, and the honestly-noted estimator-dependence and finite-sample-bias
caveats.
